q-cd-type.label: The tense pair in an if-sentence
q-cd-type.summary: Each kind of condition fixes both halves: real, likely, unlikely or impossible.

q-cd-wish.label: Wish, as if, if only
q-cd-wish.summary: These take the past form for the present and 'were' for every subject.

q-cd-unless.label: Unless, in case, provided
q-cd-unless.summary: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so a second negative is wrong.

q-cd-connector.label: As soon as, before, after, until, when, provided
q-cd-connector.summary: Not just 'if' — as soon as, before, after, until, when, provided and lest all refuse 'will/shall' in their own clause; the future sits only in the other half.

rules.text: A general truth takes the present in both halves: If you heat ice, it melts. A likely future takes the present in the if-half and will in the other: If it rains, we will stop. Never put 'will' in the if-half.
rules.ok: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the match.
rules.bad: If it will rain tomorrow, we will cancel the match.

rules.text: For something unlikely or imaginary now, use the past in the if-half and would + base verb in the other: If I had a car, I would drive. 'Were' is used for every subject: If I were you.
rules.ok: If I were the minister, I would publish the file.
rules.bad: If I was the minister, I will publish the file.

rules.text: For something that did not happen, use the past perfect in the if-half and would have + past participle in the other: If I had known, I would have come. Never 'would have' in the if-half.
rules.ok: If he had left earlier, he would have caught the train.
rules.bad: If he would have left earlier, he would have caught the train.

rules.text: After wish, if only and as if, the verb steps one tense back: a present wish takes the past, a past regret takes the past perfect, and 'were' is used for every subject.
rules.ok: I wish I were taller. He talks as if he were the owner.
rules.bad: I wish I am taller. He talks as if he is the owner.

rules.text: 'Unless' means 'if not', so the clause after it stays positive. 'Lest' is followed by should, and 'in case' and 'provided' take the present.
rules.ok: You will fail unless you work. Take an umbrella in case it rains.
rules.bad: You will fail unless you do not work.

rules.text: A clause introduced by as soon as, before, after, until, when, provided or lest never takes will/shall for a future idea; it stays in the simple present (or the present perfect, for something that must finish first). The future tense belongs only in the sentence's other half.
rules.ok: She will come to meet you as soon as you reach Delhi.
rules.bad: She will come to meet you as soon as you will reach Delhi.

q-cd-type.cue: An if-clause with a blank in one of the two halves.
q-cd-type.standard: Read the half that is complete, name the type from it, then fill the other half with the form that type requires.
q-cd-type.fast: Past in the if-half means 'would' in the other; past perfect means 'would have'.
q-cd-type.eliminate: Cross out any option that puts 'will' or 'would have' inside the if-half.
traps: 'If I will' and 'if he would have', which are never right.
'Was' instead of 'were' in an imaginary condition.
A mixed sentence where the two halves belong to different types.

q-cd-wish.cue: wish, if only or as if, followed by a blank.
q-cd-wish.standard: Step the verb one tense back from the time meant, and use 'were' for every subject.
q-cd-wish.fast: A wish about now takes the past; a wish about the past takes 'had'.
q-cd-wish.eliminate: Drop the present forms: after 'wish' they are always wrong.
traps: 'I wish I am' and 'as if he is'.

q-cd-unless.cue: unless, lest, in case or provided in the sentence.
q-cd-unless.standard: Replace 'unless' with 'if not' in your head and see whether the sentence still makes sense.
q-cd-unless.eliminate: Remove options that double the negative.
traps: 'Lest ... not', which repeats the negative already in 'lest'.

q-cd-connector.cue: as soon as / before / after / until / when / provided, with 'will' or 'shall' appearing in the same clause.
q-cd-connector.standard: Find the connector's own clause and check it for will/shall; if present, change the verb to the simple present (or present perfect for a completed-first idea).
q-cd-connector.fast: as soon as / before / after / until / when / provided + will = always wrong; drop the 'will'.
q-cd-connector.eliminate: Rule out any option that keeps 'will' or 'shall' inside the connector's own clause.
traps: The sentence clearly describes the future, so 'will' feels needed everywhere, but only one half of the sentence is allowed to carry it.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be called off.
practice.why: A likely future takes the present tense in the if-half and 'will' in the other half.

a.note: 'If it will rain' puts 'will' inside the if-half, which English never does.

c.note: The past 'rained' would make the condition imaginary, but the other half has 'will', not 'would'.

d.note: 'Would rain' belongs to an imaginary condition and clashes with 'will be called off'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If I ___ you, I would accept the transfer.
practice.why: An imaginary condition uses 'were' for every subject, and the other half has 'would'.

a.note: 'If I was you' is common in speech, but the imaginary condition takes 'were'.

c.note: The present 'am' cannot go with 'would accept'.

d.note: 'Will be' puts a future form inside the if-half.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If she had revised the chapter, she ___ the question.
practice.why: The if-half is in the past perfect, so the other half takes 'would have' plus the past participle.

a.note: 'Would answer' belongs with a simple past in the if-half, not a past perfect.

b.note: 'Will answer' cannot follow a past perfect condition.

d.note: Repeating 'had answered' leaves the sentence without a result clause.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
If he would have informed us / about the change in time, / we could have arranged / another vehicle.
options: If he would have informed us
practice.why: The if-half of an impossible condition takes the past perfect: 'If he had informed us'. 'Would have' never goes inside the if-clause.

b.note: 'About the change in time' is a correct prepositional phrase.

c.note: 'We could have arranged' is a correct result clause for this type.

d.note: 'Another vehicle' is the object and holds no error.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I wish I ___ how to swim.
practice.why: A wish about the present steps the verb back to the past.

a.note: 'Wish I know' keeps the present tense, which 'wish' does not allow.

c.note: 'Have known' is the present perfect and does not follow 'wish' here.

d.note: 'Will know' puts a future form after 'wish'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He behaves as if he ___ the owner of the shop.
practice.why: After 'as if' the verb steps back and takes 'were' for every subject.

a.note: 'As if he is' keeps the present, which the pattern does not allow.

b.note: 'Was' is heard in speech, but 'as if' takes 'were' whatever the subject.

d.note: 'Will be' puts a future form after 'as if'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If only she ___ told us earlier, we could have helped.
practice.why: 'If only' about the past takes the past perfect: 'if only she had told us'.

a.note: 'Has told' is the present perfect and clashes with 'could have helped'.

c.note: 'Would have told' in the if-half is the same error as 'if he would have'.

d.note: 'Have told' does not agree with the singular 'she'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
You will not be allowed in ___ you carry the pass.
practice.why: 'Unless' means 'if not', which is exactly what the sentence needs before a positive verb.

b.note: 'Until' is about time, not about a condition.

c.note: 'If not you carry' is not the English word order; 'if you do not carry' would be, but that is not the option.

d.note: 'Lest' is followed by 'should' and expresses a precaution.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The guard warned us / that we would be fined / unless we did not move / the car at once.
practice.why: 'Unless' already carries the negative, so 'unless we did not move' says the opposite of what is meant; it should be 'unless we moved'.

a.note: 'The guard warned us' is a correct main clause.

b.note: 'That we would be fined' is correct reported speech after a past verb.

d.note: 'The car at once' is the object with a phrase of time.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If you heat water to a hundred degrees, it ___.
practice.why: A general truth takes the present tense in both halves.

a.note: 'Will boil' turns a standing fact into a single future event; a general truth takes the present.

c.note: The past 'boiled' does not state a general truth.

d.note: 'Would boil' belongs to an imaginary condition.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She will come to meet you as soon as the train ___ at the station.
practice.why: 'As soon as' never takes will/shall in its own clause; the future belongs only in the other half.

a.note: 'As soon as the train will arrive' puts 'will' inside the connector's clause, which is never allowed.

c.note: The past 'arrived' does not fit a sentence about the future.

d.note: 'Would arrive' belongs to an imaginary condition, not this plain future plan.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Before the police will come / to take his statement, / the injured man / had already died.
practice.why: 'Before' never takes will/shall for a future idea; it should be 'Before the police come' or 'came'.

c.note: A correct subject for the main clause.

d.note: The past perfect is correctly used for the earlier of two past actions once the first part is fixed.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I shall support him so long as he ___ honest in his dealings.
practice.why: 'So long as' behaves like 'as soon as' and refuses will/shall in its own clause; it stays in the simple present.

a.note: 'So long as he will remain' puts 'will' inside the connector's clause, which the rule never allows.

c.note: The past 'remained' does not fit a sentence about ongoing support in the present and future.

d.note: 'Would remain' belongs to an imaginary condition, not this plain statement.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
There will be a rush at the counter when the sale [[will begin]].
practice.why: 'When' refuses will/shall in its own clause for a future idea; it stays in the simple present: begins.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: The past 'began' does not fit a sentence about the future.

d.note: 'Would begin' belongs to an imaginary condition, not this plain future statement.
